candidate_findings.title: Project-switch determinism lacks a transaction contract
candidate_findings.gap: The section says switching propagates across project-scoped configuration, sessions, terminal cwd, browser preview state, and effective tool, MCP, and Persona state, then declares missing-path, duplicate-path, and in-flight-run behavior deterministic without defining that behavior.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A partially applied or racing switch can leave visible shell state associated with one project while commands, credentials, sessions, or tools remain authoritative for another project.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: The requested, validating, switching, committed, failed, and cancelled states; the commit point and propagation order; old-versus-new project authority during the transition; ownership of in-flight runs and background activity; and the exact outcome for each named invalid or failure case.

evidence_refs.excerpt: - default switch target is the active workspace tab only - an alternate command opens the target project in a new workspace tab - switching recalculates project-scoped config, sessions, terminal cwd, browser preview state, and effective tool/MCP/persona state - background activity from the old project remains visible through badges/attention surfaces - missing-path, duplicate-path, and in-flight-run behavior are deterministic and user-visible

candidate_findings.title: Hot-reload and live-reload lifecycle is not executable
candidate_findings.gap: The section requires stack awareness, visible fallback, launch status, errors, termination, and cleanup, but does not define the lifecycle that connects those requirements.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Different callers can classify the same stack differently, leave duplicate watchers or child processes running, reuse occupied ports, or display live-reload state after the underlying dev session has failed.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Caller authority; stack-detection authority and confidence; eligibility and fallback triggers; dev-session states and guarded transitions; watcher, child-process, and port ownership; termination timeout and escalation; cleanup outcomes on project switch or shutdown; and scenario-level pass/fail oracles.

evidence_refs.excerpt: - dev sessions are stack-aware and distinguish hot reload from live reload when the stack supports both - fallback to live reload is explicit in UI copy and state - one-click launch, status, logs, errors, and termination rules are required - project switch and app shutdown use explicit termination/cleanup rules

candidate_findings.title: Browser-context chip revocation has no atomic lifecycle
candidate_findings.gap: The visible-chip model prohibits hidden injection and prohibits blocked, expired, or revoked chips from serializing successfully, but it does not define when chip state is evaluated or how revocation races prompt construction and dispatch.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A chip revoked after prompt compilation but before dispatch could still disclose page, selection, element, or screenshot-derived context despite the GUI showing it as revoked.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Stable chip identity and source-session binding; captured-content immutability or staleness after navigation; created, blocked, expired, revoked, serialized, and dispatched transitions; transition authority; expiry calculation; the atomic boundary between attachment validation and prompt dispatch; and audit/retention behavior for failed serialization.

evidence_refs.excerpt: - Browser click/highlight/share flow MUST use an explicit chip-based model: browser-derived context enters a thread only through visible, user-triggered chips, never through hidden automatic context injection. - Browser capture is split into two browser-specific attachment paths: text selection creates `browser_selection_context`, and element pick creates `browser_element_context`. - Browser screenshot and combined selection+screenshot actions create runtime-artifact references plus the selected browser context chip; they MUST NOT inject raw unbounded page bodies, DOM dumps, or screenshots directly into prompt text. - `cmd.browser.share_with_agent` and `cmd.browser.revoke_share_with_agent` update explicit browser-session share state only; sharing a browser subject does not serialize page, selection, or element context unless a separate visible capture chip is created. - Blocked, expired, or revoked browser chips may remain visible for audit, but they MUST NOT serialize as successful prompt attachments.

candidate_findings.title: Browser-action grammar and partial-failure semantics are incomplete
candidate_findings.gap: The canonical action-table columns, a small generic field list, output-section examples, and sequential execution rules do not form a discriminator-complete request and result contract. The isolated `5 MB default` has no identified subject, and sequential execution has no specified behavior after timeout, invalid input, cancellation, or runtime failure.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Callers and runtimes can disagree about required payloads, budget accounting, whether later actions execute after a failure, and whether partial artifacts or side effects are authoritative.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Required and forbidden fields for each action type; the object governed by the 5 MB limit; structured success, error, and partial-result shapes; timeout clock and nesting rules; stop-versus-continue behavior; cancellation and cleanup semantics; side-effect and artifact preservation; retry/idempotency rules; and deterministic test oracles for each failure position in an action array.

evidence_refs.excerpt: The canonical browser action table schema uses these columns at minimum: `action_id`, `bucket`, `tier` (`guaranteed_everyday` or `advanced_debug_testing`), `permission_layer`, `allowed_session_classes`, `requested_capabilities`, `artifacts_emitted`, `degradation_or_blocking_behavior`, and `user_visible_entry_points`.

Browser runtime output MUST separate structured page snapshots for actioning from screenshots for evidence/visual output. Action results may expose typed browser-output sections such as `Open tabs`, `Page state`, `Snapshot`, `New console messages`, `Modal state`, and `Downloads` rather than one flat opaque blob.

Fields: - value?: string - description?: string - timeout_ms - type: "click" | "scroll" | "type" | "press_key" | "wait_for" | "navigate" | "screenshot" | "set_viewport" | "fill_form" | "select_option" | "back" | "reload" | "snapshot" | "console" | "network"

Rules: - invalid_input - 5 MB default - timeout_ms defaults to 5000ms; max 30000ms; total across all actions capped at 30s - Unknown `type` values → `invalid_input` error - Actions are executed sequentially in array order - reject non-HTTP(S) schemes - default to `https://` if bare domain - reject malformed URLs

candidate_findings.title: Automation-to-normal-browser promotion lacks a data-transfer boundary
candidate_findings.gap: Promotion is user-confirmed and profile isolation is required, but `eligible browser state` is undefined and there is no contract for selecting, previewing, merging, or failing the transfer into a persistent profile.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Promotion can unintentionally persist authentication cookies, local storage, browsing history, permissions, or other sensitive automation state, or overwrite newer state already present in the destination profile.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: The exact eligible and prohibited state classes; source and destination identities; user-visible disclosure of what will be copied; conflict and merge behavior; transaction and rollback boundaries; provenance and audit records; failure outcomes; and the effect on restore, revocation, and subsequent profile writes.

evidence_refs.excerpt: Persistence + isolation: browser history, cookies, storage, auth sessions, per-project isolation, restore eligibility, and crash recovery are explicit browser-session state. Normal browser sessions are project-scoped, while `automation_session` and `auth_session` remain isolated unless user-confirmed promotion or state copy changes profile/restore behavior.

user-confirmed promotion from paused automation into normal browsing copies or promotes eligible browser state into the normal persistent profile/store, converts or reclassifies the visible automation browser as a normal browser tab/session, and changes future restore behavior because the session is no longer treated as automation; promotion or state copy must be an explicit user action, never a hidden side effect

Persistent profiles are scoped by profile name and project; `profile: { name: string, saveChanges: boolean }` never allows cookies or localStorage to bleed into another profile scope, and disabled `saveChanges` keeps the session isolated even when it began from a named profile.

candidate_findings.title: Shared persistent browser profiles lack concurrency semantics
candidate_findings.gap: Named profiles can write cookies and localStorage back, while detached preview shares the originating workspace-preview profile and state. The assigned range does not define concurrent-writer or cross-process consistency behavior.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Simultaneous normal or detached sessions can lose updates, resurrect deleted credentials, produce inconsistent logout state, or expose stale authorization state across windows.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Profile-store locking and ownership; snapshot/version semantics; conflict detection and merge policy; concurrent `saveChanges` behavior; cookie and storage deletion propagation; crash-safe persistence; quota and eviction behavior; and the visible failure state when the store cannot be committed.

evidence_refs.excerpt: - Browser-session options include persistent profiles through `profile: { name: string, saveChanges: boolean }`; `saveChanges` determines whether cookies and localStorage are written back after the session so authenticated workflows can persist intentionally, while `/localStorage` slash notation remains lineage for the canonical `localStorage` storage field. - Normal browser sessions are project-scoped persistent profile/store subjects: `workspace_preview` uses the project profile; `detached_preview` shares the originating `workspace_preview` profile/state unless explicitly opened as a separate browsing session; `automation_session` uses a separate ephemeral profile by default; and `auth_session` uses a separate isolated auth profile/store.

candidate_findings.title: Browser runtime restart and update policy is named but not specified
candidate_findings.gap: The section requires crash detection, restart policy, sandboxing, update rules, signature/hash verification, uninstall behavior, and a platform guarantee matrix, but does not state their operational semantics.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A helper crash loop, incompatible CEF update, failed signature check, or partial uninstall can strand sessions, corrupt runtime state, or silently change effective capabilities across platforms.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Runtime and wrapper version compatibility; atomic installation and activation; update rollback; behavior of active sessions during update or removal; health thresholds; retry, backoff, and crash-loop limits; sandbox initialization failure; process ownership; diagnostic retention; and platform-specific acceptance thresholds.

evidence_refs.excerpt: - Runtime/process lifecycle: PM-managed browser helpers use a helper/subprocess layout with `/subprocess` startup, shutdown, crash detection, restart policy, sandboxing, and diagnostics surfaces. Failures surface as requested/effective runtime state instead of silent fallback. - Distribution + runtime layout: per-platform runtime bundle layout, update rules, signature/hash verification with `/hash` evidence, and uninstall/removal behavior with `/removal` evidence are required for macOS, Linux, and Windows packages. - Platform guarantee matrix: Linux/macOS/Windows guarantees are explicit; capability differences may be degraded-but-supported only when effective capability loss is disclosed before use.

candidate_findings.title: Terminal identity and restore rules lack a guarded state machine
candidate_findings.gap: The section lists lifecycle events, identity invariants, liveness verification, and restore outcomes, but does not define the authoritative terminal-session states or the guarded transitions connecting them.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Concurrent reveal, restart, kill, detach, reattach, restore, and process-exit events can duplicate shells, target a replacement session with a stale command, or show historical state as live.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: The complete session-state set; event preconditions and transition authority; ordering and conflict rules for concurrent lifecycle commands; the meaning and lifetime of session existence; the liveness-verification method and timeout; mapping from verification results to restore outcomes; stale-identity rejection; and user-visible state for ambiguous or failed restoration.

evidence_refs.excerpt: structured-event recording includes session create, `/attach/ready/start-command/finish-command`, interrupt, `/terminate/kill`, detach, `/reattach/move-window`, resize, `/focus/visibility`, cwd/profile changes, renderer errors, shell-integration state changes, selection and clipboard failures, and capability fallback for `/render/integration` diagnostics.

- same-session reveal never spawns a duplicate shell when the referenced `terminal_session_id` still exists - restarting a session mints a new `terminal_session_id`; clearing scrollback does not - restored historical sessions never fake live PTY continuity
terminal sessions and dev sessions have explicit restore eligibility; a running process is never assumed alive after restart without verification
Canonical restore outcomes are: - `restored_live` - `restored_exited` - `restored_disconnected` - `restored_without_history`
terminal restart or replacement creates a new `terminal_session_id`; restoring a historical pane never synthesizes that new identity automatically

candidate_findings.title: Terminal responsiveness and bounded-memory requirements lack measurable oracles
candidate_findings.gap: The section requires replay fixtures, platform performance tests, instrumentation, and responsive bounded-render and bounded-memory behavior, but supplies no quantitative pass/fail boundaries.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Implementations with materially different memory growth, latency, frame loss, selection stability, or search behavior can all claim compliance with qualitative terms such as responsive, huge output, and bounded.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Fixture sizes and output rates; transcript and memory ceilings; parser, buffer, search, persistence, input, frame, and resize latency budgets; dropped/deferred-paint limits; observation duration and percentile rules; platform-specific thresholds; overload degradation behavior; and the oracle for selection, cursor, and scroll-anchor stability.

evidence_refs.excerpt: Parser-engine gates cover `/VT` escape parsing, `/ANSI/grid/buffer` state, `/selection/scroll` anchor stability, and regression-tested replay fixtures for command blocks, alternate-screen transitions, huge output, search, and resize.

Platform performance tests cover WSL, `/Windows/Wayland/macOS`, IME behavior, GPU fallback, `/PTY` resize/focus/attach paths, and `/compositing/scrolling`; GPU can help grid drawing, but it never rescues a weak terminal-model architecture.

Terminal performance instrumentation includes PTY input/output throughput indicators, parser/buffer latency, frame/render timing, dropped/deferred paint counters, search latency on large retained transcript, and transcript flush/persist latency.
huge-output, search, and scrollback paths remain responsive under bounded-render and bounded-memory rules

candidate_findings.title: Terminal diagnostic-bundle export controls are incomplete
candidate_findings.gap: The section separates metadata logging from transcript capture and requires explicit transcript inclusion, but does not define who may request or approve a bundle, what redaction occurs, where the bundle can go, or how long it remains accessible.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Terminal diagnostics can contain commands, paths, environment-derived values, project identifiers, error payloads, and transcript excerpts that expose secrets or private user activity.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Requester and approver authority; confirmation timing; secret, path, environment, and transcript redaction rules; destination and recipient constraints; encryption and access control; retention and deletion; project and session boundary enforcement; audit events; and failure behavior for incomplete or oversized bundles.

evidence_refs.excerpt: Diagnostic logging records terminal subsystem events and failures as metadata, state transitions, failure codes, and performance counters; it must not indiscriminately capture or duplicate full shell content. Transcript capture remains a terminal review feature, not a blanket debug log sink, and logging boundaries distinguish metadata-only artifacts from transcript-including artifacts without unexpectedly exporting sensitive command content/environment data unless the user explicitly chooses that artifact class.

PM can produce a terminal diagnostic bundle per pane/session/project on request. Bundle contents may include structured lifecycle/error events, renderer/capability/settings state, settings relevant to terminal behavior, and optional transcript excerpts only when explicitly included; support bundles clearly label transcript content as absent, partial, or included.

candidate_findings.title: Sound policy lacks state, precedence, and test semantics
candidate_findings.gap: The section groups sound effects into settings and says notifications respect do-not-disturb or muted state, but does not define the policy that determines whether a sound fires.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Concurrent sessions and conflicting OS, shell, application, project, or event-category settings can produce unexpected or repeated sounds, including during accessibility-sensitive or presentation contexts.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Defaults and setting scope; action-needed and completion event classification; precedence among OS do-not-disturb, shell mute, application mute, and per-project preferences; transition propagation; duplicate-event coalescing; output-device failure behavior; accessibility alternatives; and deterministic test cases.

evidence_refs.excerpt: - sound effects are grouped as settings, not per-view ad hoc toggles - sound notifications follow action-needed / completion semantics and respect do-not-disturb or muted-state policy from the shell

candidate_findings.title: SMPFS-003 validates preservation rather than its behavioral claim
candidate_findings.gap: SMPFS-003 asserts active-project ownership, project-switch placement, and persistent visibility of background, blocked, or failed activity, but its acceptance criteria cover addressability, source preservation, and non-creation of implementation artifacts; its validation surfaces are migration and index validators.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: The PlanUnit can pass every listed criterion while none of its user-visible shell behavior, ownership invariants, or failure-state visibility is demonstrably testable.
candidate_findings.missing_or_underspecified: Behavioral acceptance oracles for one-active-project ownership, project-switch scoping, persistence and correctness of background/blocked/failed indicators, and a validation surface capable of exercising those claims rather than only validating plan migration and indexing.

evidence_refs.excerpt: The app shell is workspace-tab based: each workspace tab owns one active project, project switching is a workspace-tab concern rather than a title-bar project bar, and background, blocked, or failed activity remains visible through persistent shell regions.
